paragraphs: This is the natural and unavoidable direction of even the best constituted governments. Sparta and Rome both perished, so what State can hope to last forever? If we want to build a government that endures a long time, we should not even dream of making it eternal. To succeed, we must not attempt the impossible, and we must not flatter ourselves that we can give a human creation a stability that the human condition does not allow.

The body politic, like the human body, starts dying the moment it is born, and carries the causes of its own destruction inside it. But either one may have a sturdier constitution, better suited to keep it alive for a shorter or longer time. A man’s constitution is the work of nature; the State’s is the work of art. People cannot extend their own lives, but it is up to them to extend the life of the State as far as they can, by giving it the best possible constitution. Even the best constituted State will end; but it will end later than any other, unless some unforeseen accident destroys it before its time.

The body politic draws its life from the sovereign authority. The legislative power is the heart of the State; the executive power is its brain, which sets every part moving. The brain can be paralyzed and the person still live. A man can remain feeble-minded and go on living; but once the heart stops doing its work, the animal is dead.

The State survives not through its laws but through the legislative power. A law made yesterday does not bind us today. But silence is taken as tacit consent, and the Sovereign is held to be confirming, at every moment, the laws it could repeal and does not. Whatever it has once declared that it wills, it goes on willing, unless it revokes the declaration.

Why, then, do we show so much respect for old laws? For this very reason. We have to believe that only the excellence of the old acts of will could have kept them alive so long: had the Sovereign not found them wholly beneficial, it would have revoked them a thousand times. So in any well constituted State the laws do not weaken; they keep gaining strength, because the precedent of age makes them more venerable every day. But wherever laws grow weak as they grow old, that proves there is no longer a legislative power, and that the State is dead.
